newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh to ask $2 billion in foreign aid.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to ask $2 billion in foreign aid.

text.p: Bangladesh's finance minister leaves for Paris on Saturday with hopes of getting up to $2 billion in aid from the annual aid consortium meeting, finance officials said on Friday.
Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria will attend the three-day meeting in the French capital sponsored by the World Bank.
Finance officials said the meeting, which begins on Monday, was crucial for the 10-week-old government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to implement economic reforms and development.

Kibria told a seminar in Dhaka on Thursday that his government would complete economic reform programmes in phases and make timely use of aid money. He called for cooperation from everyone, especially the country's restive opposition.
Pierre Landell-Mills, the World Bank mission chief in Dhaka, said before leaving for Paris that he hoped Bangladesh's new government would "reactivate the unfinished reform programmes."
"This is the expectation of the donors," he told Reuters. "I am very hopeful about the success of the Paris meeting."

Finance ministry officials said Dhaka would seek the disbursement of at least $1.7 billion during fiscal 1996-97 (July-June), including $1.3 billion in project aid, $260 million in commodity assistance and the rest for food import.
Donor countries and agencies committed $1.95 billion for Bangladesh in 1995-96 but actual disbursement was $1.59 billion.
If the new government fails to receive the aid, it would be difficult to finance development activities, the officials said.
Some 43 percent of Bangladesh's development fundings came from local resources in 1995-96. That is expected to reach 47 percent in the coming year.
"Still, the lion's share (of the development funds) has to come through foreign assistance," one official told Reuters.
Landell-Mills said the donors had been "very flexible" towards the new government.
"This government has been elected democratically and appears committed to finish the remaining reform programmes," he said without elaborating.
Hasina became chief executive after the June 12 general election returned her Awami League to power 21 years after it was ousted in a military coup.
Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the man who led Bangladesh to independence from Pakistan in 1971, was killed with most members of his family in the August 15, 1975 coup.
Hasina has promised to rid the country of illegal arms and violence and to pursue a free market economy and privatisation, which drew applause from donors and investors.
Kibria said Bangladesh would stress its "priorities for aid" at the consortium meeting.

Landell-Mills said the World bank would not recommend any fixed aid package for Bangladesh, but will leave it to the donors to consider the country's economic needs, success and failure in reforms, and its commitments for the future.
